student.headline: Work only with permission: secure the vehicle, control every energy source and keep the bay clear.
hazards: Vehicles and heavy components can move, fall or crush.
Rotating, hot, sharp or pressurised parts can injure you.
Fuel, batteries, oils, cleaners, fumes and dust can burn, poison or start a fire.
Tools, hoses, leads and spills can create impact, cut, slip and trip hazards.
beforeStart: Complete the automotive workshop induction and identify exits, alarms, emergency stops, spill kit and first-aid location.
Wear task-appropriate PPE, tie back hair and remove jewellery or loose clothing.
Get teacher permission and identify the vehicle’s fuel, electrical, pneumatic, hydraulic, spring and gravity hazards.
Check the bay, tools, guards, supports and ventilation before work starts.
dos: Keep the ignition/key under teacher control and prevent unexpected vehicle movement.
Use the correct SOP, tool and support method for each task.
Keep parts, hoses, leads and spills out of walkways; clean as you go.
Stop, isolate and ask the teacher before changing the task or clearing a fault.
donts: Do not start or move a vehicle, use a hoist, jack, powered tool or hazardous product without permission.
Do not work beneath a vehicle or suspended component unless an approved support system is correctly engaged.
Do not bypass guards, safety locks, extraction, fuses or isolation steps.
Do not run, distract others, wear headphones or use compressed air to clean skin or clothing.
stop: The vehicle or load moves, settles or is not securely supported.
You find an unknown battery, orange high-voltage cable, airbag component, fuel leak or suspected asbestos material.
There is smoke, fire, a strong odour, fluid under pressure, damaged equipment or failed extraction.
Someone enters the exclusion zone or anything differs from the teacher’s demonstrated setup.
student.note: Published Student safety summary. This page supports safety awareness and does not by itself authorise a practical task. Teacher instruction, permission, active supervision, the exact vehicle or equipment instructions, local RAMS and school procedures remain authoritative.

teacher.overview: General entry and conduct controls for an educational automotive workshop. Task-specific SOPs, vehicle service information, equipment manuals, hazardous-substance controls and local RAMS remain necessary.
hazards: Vehicles and heavy components can move, fall or crush.
Rotating, hot, sharp or pressurised parts can injure you.
Fuel, batteries, oils, cleaners, fumes and dust can burn, poison or start a fire.
Tools, hoses, leads and spills can create impact, cut, slip and trip hazards.
riskAssessment: Treat each vehicle as a system containing multiple energy sources and stored energy; a key removed from the ignition is not a complete isolation.
Young or inexperienced learners require task boundaries, demonstrated competence and supervision matched to the consequences of failure.
preStart: Complete a task-specific assessment of vehicle condition, energy sources, products, lifting/support requirements and student capability.
Control vehicle access and keys; establish exclusion zones and verify emergency equipment, ventilation and housekeeping.
safeUse: Apply the hierarchy of controls before relying on PPE.
Use the documented isolation method for the vehicle and task; release or secure stored energy and test the isolation where applicable.
Maintain supervision, safe separation and housekeeping for the whole lesson.
shutdown: Return all controls to a safe state, account for tools and parts, remove waste and spills, and leave the vehicle securely parked.
Record faults, incidents, near misses and any equipment removed from service.
restrictions: This general SOP does not authorise high-voltage EV/HEV work, pyrotechnic restraint systems, refrigerant work, spring compressors, tyre machines, hoists or hot work.
Any restricted process requires its own approved SOP, competent supervision and suitable equipment.
disposal: Segregate used oils, coolants, fuels, contaminated absorbents, batteries, metal and general waste under the local hazardous-waste plan.
storage: Store chemicals in labelled compatible containers and secured cabinets; store keys, lifting accessories, tools and chargers to prevent unauthorised use.
furtherInformation: Map the actual workshop equipment to the SOP library before starting a new unit.
firstAid: Stop work, isolate energy only if it is safe to do so, alert the teacher and follow the PHS emergency and first-aid procedure.
For serious injury, fire, hazardous exposure or breathing difficulty, call emergency services and preserve the scene when safe.
teacherChecks: Check the exact vehicle/equipment manufacturer information and the task-specific local RAMS before the lesson.
Confirm guards, isolation, ventilation/extraction, PPE, emergency equipment, supervision and student competency are appropriate.
Remove defective or uncertain equipment from service; do not improvise a repair or control.

student.headline: Do not perform brake or clutch dust work until the teacher has confirmed the material and approved the method.
hazards: Older or imported brake pads, linings and clutch parts may contain asbestos.
Asbestos fibres are too small to see and can cause serious disease years after exposure.
Brushing, dry wiping or compressed air can spread harmful dust through the workshop.
beforeStart: Do not use, disturb or clean a suspect friction component.
Ask the teacher to confirm the part’s identity and whether an approved asbestos-free learning task is available.
Keep other people away from any damaged or dusty suspect material.
dos: Follow the teacher’s controlled wet-cleaning or suitable vacuum method only after the material has been confirmed and the task approved.
Treat unknown friction materials as suspect and report them immediately.
Keep removed parts and contaminated cleaning materials contained as directed.
donts: Do not use compressed air, a brush, dry rag or ordinary vacuum on brake or clutch dust.
Do not sand, grind, drill, break or otherwise disturb suspect asbestos material.
Do not take contaminated clothing, dust, parts or waste out of the controlled area.
stop: The age, origin or composition of the friction material is unknown.
You see damaged, loose or dusty friction material.
Dust is released, containment fails or the specified control equipment is unavailable.
Anyone may have been exposed.

teacher.overview: Awareness and stop-work controls for possible asbestos-containing composite friction materials in automotive components. Suspect material is not a normal student task.
hazards: Inhalation of asbestos fibres from friction materials can cause fatal disease after a long latency period.
Secondary contamination can expose other students, staff and cleaners.
riskAssessment: Eliminate exposure by identifying and replacing suspect components before student activity wherever reasonably practicable.
Do not infer that a part is asbestos-free from appearance alone; use reliable documentation or competent assessment.
preStart: Check vehicle/component age, origin, supplier information and the current WorkSafe inspection guidance.
Exclude students from suspect material and establish the school asbestos response/management process.
safeUse: Do not use compressed air, brushing or dry cleaning on suspect friction material.
Arrange competent assessment and any required asbestos work under current New Zealand requirements.
If RPE is required for an authorised task, select it through a competent assessment; AS/NZS 1715 selection/use and AS/NZS 1716 performance, fit testing, facial-hair compatibility and training apply.
shutdown: Contain the area and materials, prevent re-entry and follow the asbestos management/emergency procedure after any suspected release.
restrictions: Students must not remove, abrade, clean or dispose of suspected asbestos-containing components.
An RPE icon or respirator does not make unapproved asbestos work safe.
disposal: Treat suspect asbestos components and contaminated materials as asbestos waste; use an authorised disposal pathway and required documentation.
storage: Quarantine suspect components in sealed, identified packaging in a controlled location pending competent advice.
furtherInformation: The supplied CLEAPSS entry was a source lead only; its UK exposure limits, regulations and mask terminology have not been carried into this NZ SOP.
firstAid: If a release or suspected exposure occurs, stop work, keep people out, avoid further disturbance and notify the teacher/management immediately.
Seek competent asbestos advice; record the incident and follow the school exposure and emergency procedures.
teacherChecks: Check the exact vehicle/equipment manufacturer information and the task-specific local RAMS before the lesson.
Confirm guards, isolation, ventilation/extraction, PPE, emergency equipment, supervision and student competency are appropriate.
Remove defective or uncertain equipment from service; do not improvise a repair or control.

student.headline: Identify the battery type, protect against short circuits and use only the correct charger in a ventilated area.
hazards: Lead-acid electrolyte can cause serious eye and skin burns.
A short circuit can produce very high current, molten metal, burns and fire.
Charging may release flammable gas; damaged or incorrectly charged lithium batteries can burn fiercely and release toxic smoke.
Batteries are heavy and can be damaged by dropping or incorrect lifting.
beforeStart: Get teacher permission and identify the battery chemistry, voltage, polarity and manufacturer charging instructions.
Remove jewellery and check the case, terminals, leads and charger for damage, swelling, leakage or corrosion.
Set up in the teacher-approved ventilated charging area, clear of ignition sources and combustibles.
Confirm the charger is correct and switched off or disconnected before making connections.
dos: Use insulated tools and terminal covers; keep metal objects away from the terminals.
Connect and disconnect in the sequence demonstrated by the teacher and prevent reversed polarity.
Keep the battery upright and observe it during charging.
Wash hands after handling batteries and use the approved lifting method.
donts: Do not short the terminals, bypass a fuse, smoke, create sparks or place tools on a battery.
Do not charge a hot, swollen, leaking, punctured, frozen, unidentified or otherwise damaged battery.
Do not use an improvised or incompatible charger, or leave charging unattended or overnight.
Do not open, modify, repair or dismantle a battery.
stop: The battery becomes hot, swells, hisses, leaks, smells unusual, smokes or changes shape.
The charger, lead or connection becomes hot or damaged.
There is a spark, reversed connection, acid splash or charging fault.
The battery chemistry, voltage or condition is uncertain.

teacher.overview: Safe educational handling, isolation and charging of common 12/24 V vehicle batteries. Chemistry-specific manufacturer instructions and a local charging area assessment are essential.
hazards: Lead-acid electrolyte can cause serious eye and skin burns.
A short circuit can produce very high current, molten metal, burns and fire.
Charging may release flammable gas; damaged or incorrectly charged lithium batteries can burn fiercely and release toxic smoke.
Batteries are heavy and can be damaged by dropping or incorrect lifting.
riskAssessment: Lead-acid and lithium batteries present different chemical, fire and charging hazards; the battery chemistry must be positively identified.
Low nominal voltage does not remove high-current short-circuit and arc/burn risk.
preStart: Provide the correct compatible charger, inspected leads, ventilation, acid spill response and non-combustible charging location.
Assess manual handling and secure the battery against falling or terminal contact.
safeUse: Supervise polarity verification and connections; charger output must be off before connection changes.
Control ignition sources and monitor temperature, condition and charging status.
Follow manufacturer instructions and WorkSafe advice for damaged lithium batteries; do not move a battery that is actively venting or burning unless the emergency plan specifically permits it.
shutdown: Switch off/disconnect the charger before removing leads, then secure terminal covers and return the battery to approved storage.
Clean minor corrosion or spills only under the product SDS and local spill procedure.
restrictions: Students must not fill dry batteries with acid, repair batteries, improvise chargers or work on EV/HEV traction batteries.
Damaged lithium batteries require the school emergency plan and competent advice.
disposal: Recycle batteries through an approved battery collection route; treat leaked electrolyte and contaminated absorbents as hazardous waste. Do not put batteries in general waste.
storage: Store upright, secure from impact and terminal shorting, in the chemistry-appropriate ventilated area away from heat and ignition sources.
furtherInformation: Keep SDSs for electrolyte and any battery products used in the programme.
firstAid: Stop work, isolate energy only if it is safe to do so, alert the teacher and follow the PHS emergency and first-aid procedure.
For serious injury, fire, hazardous exposure or breathing difficulty, call emergency services and preserve the scene when safe.

Confirm guards, isolation, ventilation/extraction, PPE, emergency equipment, supervision and student competency are appropriate.
Remove defective or uncertain equipment from service; do not improvise a repair or control.

student.headline: Secure the engine or vehicle, guard moving parts, connect exhaust extraction and clear the area before starting.
hazards: A vehicle or test stand can move unexpectedly when an engine starts.
Belts, fans and pulleys can catch hair, clothing, tools or fingers.
Exhaust fumes can poison; hot parts, fuel and ignition systems can burn or start a fire.
Noise and ejected parts or fluids can cause injury.
beforeStart: Get teacher permission and complete the exact start checklist.
Confirm the vehicle is secured, transmission is in the approved safe position and the parking/holding controls are applied.
Check guards, fluid levels, leaks, exhaust extraction, ventilation and the exclusion zone.
Remove tools and loose items; tie hair back and warn everyone before starting.
dos: Start only from the normal operator position or approved test control.
Keep hands, clothing, leads and tools clear of moving and hot parts.
Use tailpipe/local exhaust extraction whenever an engine runs indoors.
Monitor gauges, noises, movement, leaks and extraction continuously.
donts: Do not bypass an interlock, start in gear or reach into a running engine bay.
Do not run an engine indoors without effective exhaust capture and ventilation.
Do not refuel a running or hot engine.
Do not leave a running engine unattended.
stop: The vehicle/test stand moves or the engine speed changes unexpectedly.
Extraction fails or anyone develops headache, dizziness, nausea or breathing discomfort.
There is a fuel/fluid leak, unusual noise, vibration, smoke, overheating or fire.
A guard is missing or anyone enters the exclusion zone.
student.note: Published Student safety summary. This page supports safety awareness and does not by itself authorise a practical task. Teacher instruction, permission, active supervision, the exact vehicle or equipment instructions, local RAMS and school procedures remain authoritative.

teacher.overview: Controls for starting and running vehicles or securely mounted demonstration engines in a teaching workshop.
hazards: A vehicle or test stand can move unexpectedly when an engine starts.
Belts, fans and pulleys can catch hair, clothing, tools or fingers.
Exhaust fumes can poison; hot parts, fuel and ignition systems can burn or start a fire.
Noise and ejected parts or fluids can cause injury.
riskAssessment: Starting creates multiple simultaneous risks: movement, entanglement, exhaust, noise, heat, fuel and electrical energy.
Natural ventilation alone should not be treated as exhaust capture for indoor engine running.
preStart: Use a vehicle/test-stand-specific checklist covering restraint, neutral/park verification, guards, exhaust extraction, fuel containment, cooling and emergency shutdown.
Verify the exhaust system discharges safely outside without re-entry and that the space remains adequately ventilated.
safeUse: Keep a competent operator at the control, maintain an exclusion zone and supervise continuously.
Use remote observation or test connections where reasonably practicable instead of reaching into a running system.
Shut down before adjustments unless a documented competent-person procedure specifically requires operation.
shutdown: Stop the engine, remove/control the key or start device, allow hot parts to cool and isolate required energy before further work.
Ventilate the area and inspect for leaks, faults or loose components.
restrictions: Students must not defeat guards/interlocks, tune near exposed rotating parts or run unapproved engines.
Engine dynamometers or powered rolling-road equipment require a separate equipment-specific SOP.
disposal: Contain and dispose of leaked fluids and contaminated absorbents through approved streams.
storage: Secure keys/start controls, fuel and portable test stands against unauthorised use.
furtherInformation: Pair this page with the separate exhaust-fume SOP and the manufacturer service procedure.
firstAid: Stop work, isolate energy only if it is safe to do so, alert the teacher and follow the PHS emergency and first-aid procedure.
For serious injury, fire, hazardous exposure or breathing difficulty, call emergency services and preserve the scene when safe.

Confirm guards, isolation, ventilation/extraction, PPE, emergency equipment, supervision and student competency are appropriate.
Remove defective or uncertain equipment from service; do not improvise a repair or control.

student.headline: Identify the product, control ignition and skin contact, and contain every fluid in the correct tray and waste stream.
hazards: Petrol and some cleaners produce easily ignited vapours.
Fuels, used oils and coolants can harm skin, eyes, lungs or internal organs.
Spills can spread fire, contaminate drains and cause slips.
Hot or pressurised systems can spray fluid and cause burns.
beforeStart: Get teacher permission and read the product label/SDS and vehicle instructions.
Identify the fluid, correct container, drain point, required PPE and waste route.
Let hot systems cool and release pressure only by the approved procedure.
Remove ignition sources and place the correct drain pan and spill materials before opening anything.
dos: Keep fluids in labelled, closed, compatible containers and use the smallest practical quantity.
Avoid skin contact and wash promptly after handling used oil or chemicals.
Catch drips, clean spills immediately under teacher direction and keep fluids out of drains.
Use ventilation and the transfer method demonstrated by the teacher.
donts: Do not use petrol or fuel as a cleaner or start a siphon by mouth.
Do not mix fuels, oils, coolant, brake fluid, solvents or waste streams.
Do not open a hot cooling system or work near ignition sources.
Do not put automotive fluids or contaminated absorbents in sinks or general waste.
stop: The product is unidentified, unlabelled or the SDS is unavailable.
There is a large spill, strong vapour, fire, splash or suspected inhalation/ingestion.
A system remains hot or pressurised, or fluid sprays unexpectedly.
The correct waste container, ventilation or spill equipment is unavailable.

teacher.overview: Handling and spill controls for common automotive fuels, new/used oils, coolants and related workshop fluids.
hazards: Petrol and some cleaners produce easily ignited vapours.
Fuels, used oils and coolants can harm skin, eyes, lungs or internal organs.
Spills can spread fire, contaminate drains and cause slips.
Hot or pressurised systems can spray fluid and cause burns.
riskAssessment: Controls must be based on the actual product classification and SDS; automotive fluids are not interchangeable.
Used oil may contain harmful contaminants and should be kept off skin and managed as a controlled waste stream.
preStart: Inventory and label products, maintain SDS access, determine storage/quantity controls and segregated waste streams.
Provide compatible trays, transfer equipment, ventilation, PPE and a spill response matched to the maximum credible spill.
safeUse: Eliminate open fuel handling where practicable and control all ignition sources.
Minimise quantities and exposure time; enforce hygiene and prompt decontamination.
Do not use compressed air to transfer, atomise or clean hazardous fluids.
shutdown: Close and return containers, inspect the work area, clean tools under the approved method and record/replenish spill supplies.
restrictions: Students must not decant bulk fuel, enter vapour-contaminated areas, or respond to spills beyond their training and the local plan.
Vehicle fuel-system work beyond a small approved teaching task requires a specific RAMS.
disposal: Use clearly identified segregated waste containers and an approved hazardous-waste/recycling contractor. Never discharge fuels, oil or coolant to stormwater or drains.
storage: Store in closed, compatible, labelled containers within the required hazardous-substance cabinets/areas and quantity controls.
furtherInformation: The old supplied UK quantities and disposal instructions are intentionally not reproduced; apply current NZ hazardous-substance controls and local waste arrangements.
firstAid: Stop work, isolate energy only if it is safe to do so, alert the teacher and follow the PHS emergency and first-aid procedure.
For serious injury, fire, hazardous exposure or breathing difficulty, call emergency services and preserve the scene when safe.

student.headline: Do not run an engine indoors unless the tailpipe extraction is fitted, operating and discharging safely outside.
hazards: Carbon monoxide is poisonous and cannot be reliably seen or smelled.
Other exhaust contaminants can irritate or harm the lungs.
A loose or failed hose can release fumes into occupied areas.
Hot exhaust parts and hoses can burn.
beforeStart: Get teacher permission and connect the correct extraction adaptor before starting.
Check the hose, fan/airflow indicator, outdoor discharge and open make-up air path.
Keep doors, walkways and the hose route safe and clear.
Confirm no one is near the tailpipe or discharge point.
dos: Use source capture at the tailpipe and keep it running for the whole engine-running period.
Keep the run as short as the approved test allows and monitor the hose/airflow.
Tell the teacher immediately if you feel headache, dizziness, nausea or unusual tiredness.
Allow hot parts and the extraction adaptor to cool before removal.
donts: Do not rely on smell, an open door or a respirator instead of exhaust capture.
Do not run an engine in a closed or poorly ventilated space.
Do not disconnect extraction while the engine is running.
Do not position the outdoor discharge where fumes can re-enter a building.
stop: Extraction airflow stops, the hose leaks/disconnects or fumes may be entering the room.
Anyone develops headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion or breathing discomfort.
The engine, exhaust or hose overheats or the vehicle moves.
The outdoor discharge area becomes occupied or obstructed.

teacher.overview: Source-capture and ventilation controls for internal-combustion engine exhaust in an automotive teaching workshop.
hazards: Acute carbon-monoxide poisoning and exposure to other combustion contaminants.
Thermal burns, vehicle movement and trip hazards from extraction equipment.
riskAssessment: Eliminate indoor running where practicable. When required, use effective source capture plus adequate make-up air and safe discharge.
Do not use odour as evidence of safe air; assess whether fixed or portable monitoring is required for the actual facility.
preStart: Verify extraction airflow, hose compatibility/condition, discharge location, make-up air, emergency response and any monitoring before each session.
safeUse: Maintain source capture continuously and supervise engine operation and room occupancy.
Position hoses to avoid damage and trips, and prevent exhaust re-entry through doors, windows or air intakes.
shutdown: Stop the engine before disconnecting extraction; purge/ventilate as the local procedure requires and check for heat damage.
restrictions: No indoor engine running without proven effective extraction and ventilation.
RPE is not a substitute for controlling vehicle exhaust at source.
disposal: Replace damaged hoses/filters through the approved maintenance or waste route.
storage: Store cooled hoses and adaptors so they cannot be crushed, contaminated or used without authorisation.
furtherInformation: The old supplied UK time-based natural-ventilation allowance is intentionally not carried forward.

student.headline: Use approved lift points and rated equipment; test stability before anyone approaches or works beneath a raised vehicle.
hazards: A raised vehicle can fall, roll or shift and cause fatal crushing injuries.
Wrong lift points can damage the vehicle or cause it to slip.
Hoists, jacks, stands or locks can fail if damaged, overloaded or incorrectly positioned.
Hands, feet, tools and people can be trapped during raising or lowering.
beforeStart: Get teacher permission and follow the exact hoist/jack checklist and vehicle lift-point information.
Confirm the equipment rating, inspection status and condition are suitable for the vehicle and load distribution.
Clear the vehicle, close doors/bonnet as required, secure against rolling and establish an exclusion zone.
Position lift arms, pads, jack or stands only at approved points.
dos: Raise a short distance, stop and have the teacher verify contact and stability before continuing.
Engage the hoist’s mechanical safety locks or approved supports.
Keep everyone clear while raising or lowering and communicate before movement.
Use a jack only for lifting; support the vehicle with correctly rated stands before work beneath it.
donts: Do not go under a vehicle supported only by a jack or hydraulic pressure.
Do not exceed ratings, use makeshift blocks, lift on damaged structure or move lift points while loaded.
Do not rock the vehicle, climb on it or remove major components without reassessing balance.
Do not operate controls unless authorised and able to see the full danger area.
stop: A pad, arm, stand, wheel restraint or lift point moves or appears incorrect.
The vehicle is unbalanced, overloaded, structurally damaged or its centre of gravity will change.
A lock does not engage, equipment leaks, deforms, makes an unusual sound or lacks a current inspection status.
Anyone enters the danger area.

teacher.overview: Controls for raising and supporting vehicles with hoists, trolley jacks and axle stands in a teaching workshop.
hazards: A raised vehicle can fall, roll or shift and cause fatal crushing injuries.
Wrong lift points can damage the vehicle or cause it to slip.
Hoists, jacks, stands or locks can fail if damaged, overloaded or incorrectly positioned.
Hands, feet, tools and people can be trapped during raising or lowering.
riskAssessment: A lifting device and a support device are not automatically the same; hydraulic pressure alone is not an approved support for work beneath a vehicle.
Removing engines, gearboxes, batteries or other major components can materially change balance and lift loading.
preStart: Verify equipment rating, inspection/maintenance records, vehicle mass and lift points, floor condition and intended changes to load distribution.
Use a documented pre-use checklist and control access to operating controls.
safeUse: A competent person must direct positioning, test lift, lock engagement and stability verification.
Use secondary/approved support and restraints required by the equipment/vehicle manufacturer and local assessment.
Keep the exclusion zone clear during all movement.
shutdown: Lower onto a clear level area, remove equipment only when unloaded and return controls/keys to secure storage.
Quarantine and report any equipment that leaked, slipped, overloaded or failed a check.
restrictions: Students must not work under a vehicle supported only by a jack, operate unapproved lifting equipment or improvise supports.
Inspection pits, mobile column lifts and unusual vehicles require separate local assessment.
disposal: Dispose of contaminated hydraulic absorbents and failed lifting accessories through approved routes; prevent reuse of condemned gear.
storage: Store stands, pads, chocks and lifting accessories clean, dry, identified and protected from damage.
furtherInformation: The supplied UK LOLER/PUWER references have been removed; the local lifting-equipment inspection and maintenance programme must follow current NZ duties and competent-person advice.
firstAid: For a crushing incident, do not move the vehicle/load unless necessary to prevent immediate further harm and directed by competent emergency responders.
Call emergency services immediately, keep the area controlled and follow first-aid instructions.

student.headline: Use the correct undamaged tool, keep it square to the fastener and control the force and release path.
hazards: A slipping spanner, socket or puller can cause impact, cuts and trapped fingers.
Incorrect tools or improvised extensions can break or damage fasteners and components.
Stored force in pullers or tight fasteners can release suddenly.
Incorrect torque can cause later component failure.
beforeStart: Get teacher permission and identify the correct tool, size, drive type, puller and specified torque.
Inspect handles, jaws, sockets, ratchets and torque tools for wear, cracks or damage.
Secure and support the component; clear the force and release path.
Check the torque wrench range, units and current calibration/verification status.
dos: Seat tools fully and pull with a stable stance where practicable.
Keep puller jaws even, centred and securely engaged.
Use specified tightening sequence and torque; reset/store the torque tool as its manufacturer requires.
Return tools clean and report damage or overload.
donts: Do not use pipes, hammer blows, mismatched sockets or improvised adapters unless the approved procedure specifically provides them.
Do not use a torque wrench as a breaker bar.
Do not stand in line with a loaded puller or place fingers behind a component that may release.
Do not use damaged, rounded or incorrectly sized tools.
stop: A tool slips, flexes, cracks, jams or does not seat correctly.
The component moves, stored force is uncontrolled or the specified torque is uncertain.
The puller cannot be centred or its rating/condition is unknown.
Excessive force seems necessary.

disposal: Quarantine broken tools and dispose of sharp fragments safely.
storage: Store clean, dry and organised; protect torque tools from impact and follow calibration/verification intervals.

student.headline: Check the equipment and rated pressure, keep out of the tyre trajectory zone and never direct compressed air at a person.
hazards: Compressed air can penetrate skin and cause severe internal injury.
Hoses, fittings, tools or tyre components can whip, burst or eject parts.
Incorrect gauges or pressure can overinflate a tyre and cause failure.
Compressed air can spread harmful dust and create high noise.
beforeStart: Get teacher permission and identify the approved pressure and equipment for the task.
Inspect hose, couplings, chuck, regulator, gauge, tyre, rim and valve for damage.
Secure hoses and the work; establish the tyre trajectory exclusion zone and restraint method required.
Fit eye/hearing protection and keep bystanders clear.
dos: Use regulated pressure, an accurate gauge and the approved clip-on/remote inflation method.
Stand out of the trajectory zone and monitor pressure continuously.
Isolate and bleed pressure before disconnecting, clearing a jam or changing a tool.
Use wet wiping or a suitable vacuum for dust cleaning.
donts: Do not aim compressed air at skin, clothing, hair or another person.
Do not use compressed air to clean brake/clutch dust or unknown dust.
Do not inflate a damaged, mismatched, incorrectly seated or unidentified tyre/rim assembly.
Do not kink hoses, defeat regulators or exceed any component rating.
stop: A hose whips, coupling leaks, gauge is unreliable or pressure behaves unexpectedly.
The tyre, rim, valve or bead is damaged, distorted, mismatched or does not seat normally.
Any person enters the trajectory zone.
The correct restraint, regulator or remote gauge is unavailable.

teacher.overview: Safe use of workshop compressed air, pneumatic tools and controlled tyre inflation.
hazards: Compressed air can penetrate skin and cause severe internal injury.
Hoses, fittings, tools or tyre components can whip, burst or eject parts.
Incorrect gauges or pressure can overinflate a tyre and cause failure.
Compressed air can spread harmful dust and create high noise.
riskAssessment: Pressure must be limited to the lowest effective value and every component must be rated for it.
Tyre/rim failures can be catastrophic; damaged or multi-piece assemblies require competent specialist controls beyond this general SOP.
preStart: Maintain compressor, receiver, regulators, hoses, couplings and calibrated/verified gauges; set task-appropriate pressure limits.
Assess whether a restraint/cage and remote inflation are required for the tyre/rim assembly.
safeUse: Supervise inflation from outside the trajectory zone and prevent bypass of regulators.
Isolate and depressurise before maintenance or connection changes.
shutdown: Close/isolate the supply, bleed downstream pressure, inspect and store hoses/tools without trip or damage hazards.
restrictions: Students must not inflate split/multi-piece rims, damaged assemblies or commercial/heavy-vehicle tyres under this SOP.
Never use compressed air for body or clothing cleaning.
disposal: Quarantine damaged hoses, fittings, tyres and rims so they cannot be reused; use approved recycling/disposal.
storage: Coil hoses without tight bends, protect gauges and couplings, and secure the air system from unauthorised use.
furtherInformation: WorkSafe specifically recommends wet wiping or vacuuming rather than using compressed air to remove dust.
firstAid: Treat any suspected compressed-air injection injury as a medical emergency even if the skin wound looks small; call emergency services.
For eye or hearing injury, stop work and obtain immediate first aid/medical assessment.

student.headline: Low voltage can still deliver very high current: isolate, cover terminals, fuse test circuits and verify before touching.
hazards: Battery short circuits can cause burns, molten metal and fire.
Unexpected cranking, fans, actuators or vehicle movement can crush or entangle.
Incorrect meter settings or probe placement can damage equipment and create a fault.
Airbags, pretensioners and EV/HEV high-voltage systems may remain hazardous after normal power is switched off.
beforeStart: Get teacher permission and confirm the task is limited to the approved 12/24 V circuit.
Use the correct wiring diagram and identify batteries, capacitors, actuators and other stored energy.
Switch off, control the key and isolate as the manufacturer procedure requires; verify the safe state.
Inspect insulated leads, meter, fuse protection and terminal covers.
dos: Use fused test leads or current limiting where the teaching setup provides them.
Select the meter function and range before connecting; keep fingers behind probe guards.
Cover exposed battery terminals and keep tools/jewellery away.
Reconnect only after a teacher check that tools are removed and people are clear.
donts: Do not work on orange cables, EV/HEV traction systems, airbags, pretensioners, mains circuits or inside chargers.
Do not bypass fuses, probe unknown connectors or measure current directly across a battery.
Do not disconnect/reconnect circuits with power applied unless the approved test specifically requires it.
Do not assume a circuit is safe because it is labelled low voltage.
stop: You find orange high-voltage cable, yellow restraint connectors or an unidentified energy source.
A component moves, sparks, heats, smells, smokes or draws unexpected current.
The wiring diagram, isolation state, meter category/rating or test point is uncertain.
A battery is damaged, leaking, swollen or hot.

restrictions: This SOP excludes mains electrical work, EV/HEV traction systems, airbags, pretensioners and internal charger repair.
Only a registered electrical worker may undertake prescribed electrical work where New Zealand law requires it.

student.headline: Use only the approved cleaner in the parts washer, keep the lid/control system working and prevent skin, eye and vapour exposure.
hazards: Cleaners can irritate or burn skin and eyes and may produce harmful vapour.
Some solvents are flammable and can be ignited by sparks, flames or hot surfaces.
Spraying or compressed air can spread cleaner and contamination.
A parts washer can create splash, pinch, spill and electrical hazards.

Confirm the cleaner is approved for the machine and the part.
Check lid, pump, lead, hose, ventilation and fluid level/condition.
Put on specified PPE and place the part so it cannot fall or splash.
dos: Keep the lid as closed as the process permits and use the brush/flow gently.
Let parts drain into the washer and use trays for transfer.
Wash hands after the task and report skin contact or symptoms.
Keep ignition sources and incompatible products away.
donts: Do not add petrol, fuel, thinners or an unapproved chemical to the washer.
Do not spray cleaner, use compressed air to dry parts or direct flow at a person.
Do not put hot parts, batteries, sealed/pressurised items or reactive materials in the washer.
Do not bypass the lid, fusible link, ventilation or other safety device.
stop: The product is unidentified, the SDS is unavailable or the wrong cleaner may be present.
Ventilation/pump/lid fails, the machine leaks or fluid becomes unusually hot.
There is strong vapour, dizziness, skin/eye irritation, fire or a significant spill.
The part may react with or be damaged by the cleaner.

student.headline: Hot work needs its own permit/check: isolate energy, remove combustibles, control fumes and protect the vehicle and everyone nearby.
hazards: Sparks and hot metal can ignite fuel, trim, underseal, batteries and hidden combustibles.
Welding and cutting fumes can harm lungs; coatings may produce highly toxic contaminants.
Current, heat and voltage spikes can damage vehicle electronics or create shock/burn hazards.
Cylinders, tyres, pressurised systems and enclosed spaces can fail violently when heated.
beforeStart: Do not carry out hot work until the teacher approves the task-specific hot-work check and the separate welding/grinding SOP.
Identify and isolate batteries, fuel, LPG, refrigerant, pressure, airbags/pretensioners and hidden combustible materials.
Move the work to a detached clean part where practicable; clean coatings only by the approved method.
Set screens, extraction, fire equipment, exclusion zone and a fire watch.
dos: Use source extraction close to the fume and the PPE specified for the exact process/material.
Protect nearby people from arc radiation, sparks and noise.
Keep leads/earth return arranged as the manufacturer procedure requires and away from sensitive systems.
Inspect both sides and hidden spaces during work and the defined fire-watch period.
donts: Do not weld, cut or grind a tank, drum, fuel line or unknown sealed container.
Do not perform hot work near leaks, vapours, batteries on charge, airbags, tyres or pressurised systems.
Do not rely on a respirator instead of removing coatings and using effective extraction.
Do not leave hot material or a completed hot-work area unattended.
stop: Fuel/solvent odour, smoke, hidden heating, fire or a failed fire watch occurs.
Extraction, screening, isolation or equipment fails.
The material/coating is unknown or suspected to contain a highly hazardous substance.
A pressurised, fuelled, pyrotechnic or high-voltage system may be affected.

teacher.overview: Additional vehicle-specific controls that must be applied alongside the relevant welding, cutting or grinding SOP.
hazards: Sparks and hot metal can ignite fuel, trim, underseal, batteries and hidden combustibles.
Welding and cutting fumes can harm lungs; coatings may produce highly toxic contaminants.
Current, heat and voltage spikes can damage vehicle electronics or create shock/burn hazards.
Cylinders, tyres, pressurised systems and enclosed spaces can fail violently when heated.
riskAssessment: Prefer removing and cleaning the component before hot work; vehicles contain hidden combustible, pressurised, electrical and pyrotechnic systems.
Assess coatings and fume composition before work; extraction at source is a primary control.
preStart: Use a documented hot-work check/permit covering vehicle information, both sides of the work, isolation, cleaning, extraction, screens, fire equipment and fire-watch duration.
Confirm competent supervision and that the process-specific SOP and equipment checks are complete.
safeUse: Maintain source extraction, exclusion and fire watch; continuously inspect adjacent/hidden areas.
Follow manufacturer procedures for battery/electronic-system protection and welding return location.
shutdown: Isolate equipment, secure cylinders, remove hot waste safely and complete the defined post-work fire watch and final inspection.
restrictions: No hot work on tanks, drums, fuel containers, refrigerant systems, batteries, airbags/pretensioners, EV/HEV systems or unknown coated parts under this general SOP.
Students require the separate approved process SOP and direct supervision.
disposal: Collect hot metal, grinding dust, removed coatings and contaminated cleaning materials in compatible approved waste streams.
storage: Return hot-work equipment and cylinders under their specific SOPs; keep completed parts isolated until cool.
furtherInformation: Use the WorkSafe RPE selector only after the contaminant and other controls are assessed; fit testing and clean-shaven sealing surfaces may be required for tight-fitting RPE.
firstAid: Stop work, isolate energy only if it is safe to do so, alert the teacher and follow the PHS emergency and first-aid procedure.
For serious injury, fire, hazardous exposure or breathing difficulty, call emergency services and preserve the scene when safe.
teacherChecks: Check the exact vehicle/equipment manufacturer information and the task-specific local RAMS before the lesson.
Confirm guards, isolation, ventilation/extraction, PPE, emergency equipment, supervision and student competency are appropriate.
Remove defective or uncertain equipment from service; do not improvise a repair or control.

tools.name: Lifting engines and heavy components
sourceSheets: WorkSafe New Zealand load-lifting and rigging guidance
Equipment and vehicle manufacturer instructions

local.minimumYear: Set by the automotive programme and task risk assessment.
local.supervision: Teacher-directed lift plan and direct supervision for attachment, test lift, movement and landing.
notes: Automotive Trades publication prepared 25 Aug 2026 from the supplied RAMS source material and current WorkSafe New Zealand guidance.
Publication means the safety content is available to students. It does not replace the teacher’s check of the exact vehicle, equipment, products, room, emergency arrangements or student competence.

student.headline: Plan the lift, use rated gear and attachment points, balance the load and keep everyone out of the drop zone.
hazards: Engines, gearboxes and assemblies can fall, swing, tip or trap hands and feet.
Cranes, stands, chains, slings and attachment points can fail if damaged, overloaded or wrongly used.
Removing a heavy component can change the stability of the vehicle or stand.
Manual handling can strain the back, shoulders and hands.
beforeStart: Get teacher permission and follow a written lift plan for the exact component.
Know the load mass and centre of gravity; check crane, stand, sling/chain, attachments and ratings.
Confirm manufacturer lifting points, crane-leg position, vehicle support and clear travel path.
Set an exclusion zone and agree one person to direct the lift.
dos: Take up slack slowly, make a short test lift and verify balance/attachments before continuing.
Keep the load as low as practicable and move slowly on a suitable level floor.
Use tag/control methods approved in the lift plan; keep hands clear of pinch points.
Lower onto a stable rated stand/support before adjustment or work.
donts: Do not stand, reach or work under a suspended load.
Do not exceed ratings, side-load a crane, use makeshift attachments or shock-load lifting gear.
Do not leave a suspended load unattended.
Do not move a loaded crane over uneven floors, drains, ramps or obstructions.
stop: The load tilts, swings, snags, shifts or cannot be balanced.
A chain, sling, hook, crane, stand or lifting point is damaged, unmarked or outside rating.
The vehicle/support becomes unstable or the planned path is not clear.
Anyone enters the drop/crush zone.
student.note: Published Student safety summary. This page supports safety awareness and does not by itself authorise a practical task. Teacher instruction, permission, active supervision, the exact vehicle or equipment instructions, local RAMS and school procedures remain authoritative.

teacher.overview: Planning and controlled lifting of engines, gearboxes and other heavy automotive components using workshop cranes, stands and rated accessories.
hazards: Engines, gearboxes and assemblies can fall, swing, tip or trap hands and feet.
Cranes, stands, chains, slings and attachment points can fail if damaged, overloaded or wrongly used.
Removing a heavy component can change the stability of the vehicle or stand.
Manual handling can strain the back, shoulders and hands.
riskAssessment: The complete lifting system is limited by its lowest-rated component and by crane capacity at the selected boom extension.
Removal of a component can change vehicle and stand centres of gravity; assess both the load and what remains.
preStart: Prepare the lift plan, verify mass/centre of gravity, ratings, inspection records, lifting points, support arrangement, floor and travel path.
Assign one lift director and establish communication and exclusion controls.
safeUse: Supervise attachment, test lift, balance, travel and landing; keep the load low and no person beneath it.
Use manufacturer load charts and instructions; do not rely on appearance or assumed component mass.
shutdown: Land and secure the component on a rated stand, fully unload gear, inspect after use and record/quarantine any concern.
restrictions: Students must not direct or perform an unplanned lift, ride a load, work beneath it or use unmarked/makeshift lifting gear.
Complex rigging or lifting outside workshop-crane arrangements requires a competent lifting specialist.
disposal: Quarantine condemned lifting gear and destroy/control it so it cannot return to service; recycle/dispose through an approved route.
storage: Store cranes, stands and accessories clean, dry, identified and protected; keep inspection status traceable.
furtherInformation: Manufacturer load charts take priority; WorkSafe notes that generic sling charts may contain errors.
firstAid: For a crushing incident, call emergency services immediately and do not release or move the load unless needed to prevent immediate further harm and directed by competent responders.
Keep the scene controlled and provide first aid within training.
teacherChecks: Check the exact vehicle/equipment manufacturer information and the task-specific local RAMS before the lesson.
Confirm guards, isolation, ventilation/extraction, PPE, emergency equipment, supervision and student competency are appropriate.
Remove defective or uncertain equipment from service; do not improvise a repair or control.
